title: Trustly cuts a quarter of its workforce and compliance asks why
summary: Trustly's 200-job cut raises hard questions about compliance resourcing inside fintechs under cost pressure. Plus: a new open payments network from ex-Visa crypto leadership lands $13.5M, and overdue obligations in Hong Kong and Korea need attention before quarter-end.
script:
ALEX: I want to start with a pattern, because I think today's news tells one coherent story even though the items look unrelated on the surface. A major payments fintech cuts a quarter of its workforce. A new open payments network emerges from stealth with serious backing. And a compliance tech vendor lands more than a hundred million dollars in growth financing. Jordan, what do you see when you put those three things next to each other?

JORDAN: I see a market sorting itself out, and not gently. The fintechs that bet on volume and geography are shedding cost. The infrastructure players are consolidating. And a new entrant from credible ex-Visa leadership is trying to find a lane before the window closes. What I don't see is anyone talking about what happens to the compliance function inside Trustly when you lose one in four people.

ALEX: That's where I want to start. Trustly confirmed on the twenty-fourth that it is eliminating approximately two hundred roles, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. The stated rationale is a recalibration toward profitable geographies and a lower cost base. That framing is standard restructuring language, and on its own I wouldn't flag it.

JORDAN: But the timing matters. Trustly operates across multiple regulated jurisdictions, including markets with active AML supervisory scrutiny of payment institutions. A twenty-five percent headcount reduction is not a line-item story. It is a governance story. Who owns the financial crime programme after the cut? Which controls are now running on fewer hands than the risk assessment assumed?

ALEX: I'd push back slightly there. Headcount cuts don't automatically mean control degradation. If the firm is exiting geographies at the same time, the risk perimeter shrinks. It is possible the residual programme is appropriately sized for a smaller footprint.

JORDAN: Possible, yes. But that only holds if the compliance function was sized proportionately to geography in the first place, and if the exits are clean, meaning the correspondent relationships, the merchant portfolios, the payment flows, all actually wind down rather than migrate to another legal entity. That is the question supervisors in the UK and in the European Union will be asking, and if Trustly has a presence touching Asia-Pacific corridors, AML/CTF officers in Australia and Singapore should be reviewing their correspondent and third-party exposure to this firm right now.

ALEX: So the action item here is not to watch Trustly specifically. It's to treat any fintech counterparty that announces significant workforce restructuring as a trigger for an enhanced periodic review.

JORDAN: Exactly. If you're running correspondent banking or third-party payment relationships, the Trustly announcement is a prompt to pull that relationship file. Check when you last refreshed the AML controls assessment for that counterparty, check whether the governance structure you relied on when you onboarded them still exists. Don't wait for a regulator to ask you why you didn't notice.

ALEX: Moving on, and this one sits in different territory. A company called Atum has emerged from stealth with thirteen point five million US dollars in seed funding. It's an open payments network, and its founder is Pete Cooling, previously the head of crypto product at Visa. That combination of open infrastructure and crypto-adjacent leadership will attract regulatory attention before Atum has filed its first licence application anywhere.

JORDAN: The concern here is familiar but worth stating precisely. Open payments networks that route value across jurisdictions without a single licensed entity sitting in the middle create travel-rule complexity immediately. Under FATF Recommendation 16, the obligation sits with the originating and beneficiary virtual asset service providers. But if Atum's architecture distributes that function, you have a gap question from day one.

ALEX: And the regulator question is who supervises what. The MAS framework for payment service providers under the Payment Services Act is fairly well developed for established categories. A genuinely novel open network is harder to classify, and classification determines which Notice applies, which in turn determines your customer due diligence and transaction monitoring obligations.

JORDAN: I'd actually say the more immediate compliance question isn't the licensing category. It's the counterparty question for existing institutions. If Atum starts attracting merchant or institutional clients before its regulatory status is settled, licensed banks and payment institutions processing those flows need to have made their own determination about what risk classification applies. You can't outsource that judgment.

ALEX: Right. For any firm doing onboarding of payments infrastructure businesses right now, Atum is a good case study to bring to your new business risk committee. Not because it is necessarily high risk, but because it is genuinely novel, and novel structures deserve fresh analysis rather than a template fit.

JORDAN: Before we close on the news, the MyComplianceOffice financing is worth thirty seconds. More than a hundred million dollars from Accel-KKR Credit Partners into compliance technology infrastructure is a signal that institutional capital still sees regulatory obligation growth as durable. For heads of financial crime who are making vendor selection decisions right now, that level of backing matters for longevity assessments. It's not a story about MCO specifically. It's a data point about where the market thinks the compliance tech build-out is heading.

ALEX: Agreed, and I'll leave it there because I think it's genuinely uncontested. Shifting to obligations, two items that need attention before quarter-end. Hong Kong first. The HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual CG-5 thematic review on STR narrative quality from the fourth quarter of last year is still open for roughly a quarter of the authorised institution population. If your firm received a deficiency letter earlier this year and you haven't formally closed the findings, that is overdue at high priority.

JORDAN: The practical read on this: if you're an MLRO at an HKMA-supervised AI, the question is whether you can demonstrate to the HKMA that you've remediated the specific narrative quality issues they flagged, not just that you've run a training session. Examiners will want to see before-and-after samples, a revised quality assurance process, and sign-off at senior management level. If you haven't started that pack, start it this week.

ALEX: Korea is the second. The Financial Transaction Reports Act, Article 5-2, mandates an annual VASP travel-rule compliance review. That review was due in March, and VASPs that missed it are now exposed to enforcement from KoFIU and the FSC. If you're operating one of the four major Korean exchanges, Upbit, Bithumb, Coinone, or Korbit, or if you're a foreign VASP with Korean users, the question is whether your travel-rule vendor integration covers both inbound and outbound flows, and whether you have a documented review on file.

JORDAN: One addition on Korea. Two years into the travel-rule regime, examiners are no longer interested in whether the technology is plugged in. They want to see dispositioning rates, exception handling, and what you did with the transactions you couldn't match. If any of that process is informal or undocumented, the review is the moment to fix it.

ALEX: That's the briefing for Thursday the twenty-fifth. Full obligation register and source links are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. Jordan, closing thought?

JORDAN: The Trustly story is the one to sit with. Cost pressure on fintechs does not stay inside the fintech. It migrates to counterparty risk, to correspondent exposure, to gaps that your next examination may surface before you do. Get ahead of it.
